plants.name: Tomato
plants.tip: Cordon types need side shoots pinched out. Bush types don't.

sow.title: How to sow indoors
steps: Fill small pots or modules with seed compost, tap it level and water it before sowing.
Sow 2 seeds per pot 0.5 cm deep and cover with compost.
Keep them warm, ideally 18 to 24°C, on a sunny windowsill or in a propagator. Seedlings should appear in 7 to 14 days at 18 to 24°C.
When the first true leaves open, keep the strongest seedling and snip the rest off at soil level.
Pot on into a 9 cm pot when roots start poking out the bottom.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy and give them as much light as you can so they don't go leggy.

harden.title: Harden off
steps: About a week before planting out, start getting the plants used to life outside.
Days 1 to 2. Put them out in a sheltered, shady spot for two or three hours and bring them back in.
Days 3 to 5. Leave them out most of the day in brighter light, back in at night.
Days 6 to 7. Leave them out day and night unless frost is forecast.
Going into the tunnel? A few days sitting in the tunnel before planting is enough.
Water them well while they're outside. Pots dry out fast in the wind.

plantOut.title: How to plant out
steps: Water the plants an hour before moving them so the rootball holds together.
This is a hungry crop. Dig in a bucket of compost or well-rotted manure first.
Plant them deeper than they were in the pot, up to the first leaves. Tomatoes grow extra roots along the buried stem.
Space them 45 cm apart with rows 60 cm apart.
Tie each plant loosely to a cane, or twist it round a string tied to the tunnel frame.
Firm the soil gently around each plant and water in well.
plantOut.layout: Two staggered rows along the sunniest side of the bed, each plant with a cane or a string tied to the frame above.

care: Pinch out side shoots on cordon types every week. They grow in the joint between leaf and stem.
Water little and often at the same time each day. Uneven watering causes split fruit and blossom end rot.
Feed weekly with tomato feed once the first truss of fruit has set.
When there are six or seven trusses, pinch out the top so the plant ripens what it has.
Thirsty plant. In dry spells give it a deep soak two or three times a week rather than a sprinkle every day.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Pick when fully coloured and just slightly soft.
At the end of the season ripen green fruit indoors in a bag with a banana.

seedSaving.note: Only save seed from open-pollinated or heritage varieties. F1 hybrids don't come true from seed.

section.title: How to save seeds
steps: Pick a really ripe fruit from your best plant.
Squeeze the seeds and jelly into a jar with a splash of water.
Leave it on a windowsill for three days until a mould forms on top. This removes the gel and kills some diseases.
Rinse the seeds in a sieve until clean, then spread them on a plate (not kitchen paper, they stick).
Dry for a week, then store in a labelled paper envelope.

Sow 1 seed per pot 1 cm deep and cover with compost.
Push the seed in on its edge so water doesn't sit on the flat side and rot it.
Keep warm, about 20 to 25°C. Seedlings should appear in 4 to 7 days at 20 to 25°C.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy and give them as much light as you can so they don't go leggy.

Firm the soil gently around each plant and water in well.

Pinch out side shoots two leaves past a female flower.
Water every day in warm weather and feed every two weeks.

steps: Leave one fruit on the plant until it turns yellow and goes soft, well past eating stage.
Scoop out the seeds into a jar of water and leave for two days to ferment, like tomatoes.
Rinse, keep the seeds that sink and dry them on a plate for a week.

plants.tip: One or two plants is plenty for most families.

Space them 90 cm apart with rows 90 cm apart.
Protect young plants from slugs for the first couple of weeks.
Firm the soil gently around each plant and water in well.

care: Water at the base, never over the leaves, to avoid powdery mildew.
Feed every 10 to 14 days once fruits start.
Thirsty plant. In dry spells give it a deep soak two or three times a week rather than a sprinkle every day.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Pick at 10 to 15 cm long. Check every couple of days in summer or you'll get marrows.
The flowers are edible too. Try them stuffed or fried.

seedSaving.note: Courgettes, marrows, pumpkins and squash cross with each other, so hand pollinating is the only way to be sure. Only save seed from open-pollinated or heritage varieties. F1 hybrids don't come true from seed.

section.title: How to save seeds
steps: Pick a female flower that's about to open, tape it shut, then next morning hand pollinate it with a male flower of the same variety and tape it shut again.
Tie a label on it and let that courgette grow into a big marrow.
Leave it on the plant until the skin is hard, then store it for three more weeks.
Scoop out the seeds, rinse and dry them.

Water well once the tassels appear.

harvest: Ready when the silky tassels turn brown and a kernel pressed with your nail gives milky juice.

steps: Leave a few of the best cobs on the plant until the husks are dry and brown.
Bring them in, peel back the husks and hang them somewhere airy to dry fully.
Rub the kernels off and store them.

plants.name: Early potatoes
plants.tip: Classic Irish earlies like Home Guard are ready by late June.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Dig a trench or individual holes 12 cm deep.
Set each potato in with the shoots facing up, taking care not to snap them.
Space them 30 cm apart in rows 60 cm apart.
Cover gently with soil.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: Straight rows across the bed, 60 cm apart, so there's room to draw soil up the stems later.

care: When stems are 20 cm tall, earth them up by drawing soil over them so just the tips show.
If frost is forecast, cover any shoots with soil or fleece.
Water well once flowers appear. That's when the potatoes swell.
Hungry plant. A liquid feed every two weeks in summer gives a better crop.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Earlies are usually ready around flowering time. Scrape away some soil to check the size.
Dig in from the side of the row with a fork so you don't spear them.

section.title: How to grow more
steps: Buy fresh certified seed potatoes each year.
Home-saved tubers carry viruses and blight that build up and shrink your crop.

section.title: Chit your seed potatoes
steps: Stand the seed potatoes in egg boxes with the end that has the most eyes facing up.
Keep them somewhere bright, cool and frost free like a windowsill, porch or shed with a window.
Leave them about six weeks. They're ready when the shoots are short, sturdy and about 2 cm long.
Long pale shoots mean they're too dark. Move them somewhere brighter.

plants.name: Maincrop potatoes
plants.tip: Blight-resistant varieties like Sarpo Mira save a lot of heartache in wet summers.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Dig a trench or holes 12 cm deep.
Set each potato in with the shoots facing up.
Space them 38 cm apart in rows 75 cm apart.
Cover gently with soil.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: Straight rows 75 cm apart across the bed for earthing up.

care: Earth up the stems when they're 20 cm tall and again three weeks later.
Watch for blight in warm, wet weather (brown patches on leaves). Cut off and bin affected foliage straight away.
Water in long dry spells once flowering starts.
Hungry plant. A liquid feed every two weeks in summer gives a better crop.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: When the foliage dies back, cut it off and wait two weeks so the skins harden.
Lift on a dry day, leave them on the soil for a few hours to dry and store in paper sacks somewhere dark and frost free.

plants.name: Carrot
plants.tip: Stony or freshly manured soil makes forked carrots.

sow.title: How to sow
facts: 14 to 21 days. Slow, so keep the drill damp
steps: Rake the soil to a fine crumb and pull out any weeds and big stones.
Use the edge of a hoe or a cane to make drills 1 cm deep and 20 cm apart.
Sprinkle the seed thinly along the drill.
The seed is tiny. Mix it with a little dry sand so you can sow it thinly.
Cover with soil, firm gently with the back of the rake and water with a fine rose.
When seedlings are big enough to handle, thin them to one every 5 cm.
sow.layout: Short rows across the bed 20 cm apart. A 60 cm fleece fence or a row of onions alongside helps keep carrot fly away.

care: Thin on a calm evening and pinch off thinnings. The smell attracts carrot fly.
Weed by hand. Carrots hate competition.
Only needs watering in long dry spells.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Pull when the orange shoulders show and are the width you like.
Water the row first to make pulling easier.

seedSaving.note: Plants in this family cross easily with each other (and carrots with wild carrot). Keep only one variety flowering at a time. Only save seed from open-pollinated or heritage varieties. F1 hybrids don't come true from seed.

section.title: Saving seed next year
steps: This plant flowers in its second year. Leave a few of your best plants in the ground over winter, or replant them in spring.
Let them flower in summer. Stake the flower stems as they get tall.
When the seed heads turn brown and dry, cut them into a paper bag and hang them up to finish drying.
Rub the seed out, pick out the bits and store in labelled envelopes.

plants.name: Parsnip
plants.tip: Always buy fresh seed. Old seed rarely comes up.

sow.title: How to sow
facts: 21 to 28 days. Very slow, be patient
steps: Rake the soil to a fine crumb and pull out any weeds and big stones.
Sow 3 seeds at each spot, 15 cm apart and 1.5 cm deep.
Sow a few radish seeds along the row too. They come up fast and mark where the parsnips are.
Cover with soil, firm gently with the back of the rake and water with a fine rose.
When seedlings are big enough to handle, thin them to one every 15 cm.
sow.layout: Rows 30 cm apart with a plant every 15 cm.

care: Thin to the strongest seedling at each spot.
Only needs watering in long dry spells.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Lift from October once the leaves die back.
They taste sweeter after a frost so leave some in the ground over winter.

steps: Put the parsnip seeds in a cup of lukewarm water and leave them overnight.
It softens the seed coat and speeds up their very slow germination.
Sow them the next day while they're still plump. Don't let them dry out again.

plants.name: Beetroot
plants.tip: Boltardy is a reliable variety for early sowings.

sow.title: How to sow
steps: Rake the soil to a fine crumb and pull out any weeds and big stones.
Use the edge of a hoe or a cane to make drills 2.5 cm deep and 30 cm apart.

Let the pods go brown and crisp on the plant.
Pick, crack open and store the seeds.

plants.name: Lamb's lettuce
plants.tip: Tough little winter salad.

sow.title: How to sow

steps: Leave a few of the best flowers on the plant instead of deadheading them.
Wait until the seed heads are brown and dry. Collect on a dry afternoon.

plants.name: Celery
plants.tip: Self-blanching types are far less work.

sow.title: How to sow indoors
steps: Fill a seed tray with seed compost, tap it level and water it before sowing.
Sprinkle a pinch of seed thinly over the surface and press it in lightly. Barely cover it, the seed needs light.
When seedlings have two leaves, prick them out into modules, one per cell.
Keep them on a bright windowsill or in a propagator. Seedlings should appear in 14 to 21 days at 15 to 20°C.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy and give them as much light as you can so they don't go leggy.

harden.title: Harden off
steps: About a week before planting out, start getting the plants used to life outside.
Days 1 to 2. Put them out in a sheltered, shady spot for two or three hours and bring them back in.
Days 3 to 5. Leave them out most of the day in brighter light, back in at night.
Days 6 to 7. Leave them out day and night unless frost is forecast.
Going into the tunnel? A few days sitting in the tunnel before planting is enough.
Water them well while they're outside. Pots dry out fast in the wind.

plantOut.title: How to plant out
steps: Water the plants an hour before moving them so the rootball holds together.
This is a hungry crop. Dig in a bucket of compost or well-rotted manure first.
Dig a hole a little bigger than the pot and set the plant at the same depth it was growing.
Space them 25 cm apart with rows 25 cm apart.
Firm the soil gently around each plant and water in well.
plantOut.layout: A block 25 cm each way so the plants shade each other's stems.

care: Never let it dry out or the stems go stringy.

Hungry plant. A liquid feed every two weeks in summer gives a better crop.

plants.tip: Hates root disturbance so sow in modules.

plants.name: Onion
plants.tip: Sets are far easier than seed.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Gently push each onion set into the soil so just the tip shows. Don't screw them in.
Space them 10 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: Neat rows across the bed. A row of onions makes a good border next to carrots.

care: Check for a few weeks after planting and push back any that birds pull up.
Hand weed carefully. Onions hate competition.
Only needs watering in long dry spells.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: When the leaves flop over and turn yellow, lift them and leave them to dry in the sun for a week.
Store in nets somewhere cool and airy.

seedSaving.note: Most people just buy onion sets. Saving seed is a fun project rather than a money saver. Only save seed from open-pollinated or heritage varieties. F1 hybrids don't come true from seed.

section.title: Saving seed next year
steps: Onions flower in their second year. Replant a few good stored onions in spring.
When the big round flower heads go dry in summer, cut them into a paper bag.
Shake out the black seeds. Onion seed only keeps for a year, so sow it the next spring.

plants.name: Shallot
plants.tip: Each little bulb grows into a cluster of eight or more.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Push each shallot into the soil so the tip just shows.
Space them 20 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: Rows 30 cm apart with plants 20 cm apart along each row.

care: Push back any that birds lift.
Weed by hand.
Only needs watering in long dry spells.

Dry them in the sun, then split the clusters and store.

section.title: How to save seeds
steps: Garlic isn't grown from seed. Keep a few of your biggest, healthiest bulbs back after drying.

plants.name: Garlic
plants.tip: It needs the winter cold to split into cloves.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Split the bulb into cloves just before planting. Use only the big outer cloves.
Push each clove in pointy end up so the tip sits 2 cm below the surface.
Space them 15 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: Rows 30 cm apart across the bed.

care: Keep weed free and water in dry spells in spring.
If it sends up a curly flower stalk (a scape), snap it off and eat it.
Only needs watering in long dry spells.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Lift in late June or July when about half the leaves have gone yellow.
Dry somewhere sunny and airy for two weeks before storing.

plants.tip: Peas fix their own nitrogen so they leave the soil richer.

sow.title: How to sow
steps: Rake the soil to a fine crumb and pull out any weeds and big stones.
Use the edge of a hoe or a cane to make drills 4 cm deep and 60 cm apart.
Sprinkle the seed thinly along the drill.
Make a flat-bottomed trench 20 cm wide and sow three staggered rows of peas 7 cm apart.
Put up pea sticks or netting along the row at sowing time.
Cover with soil, firm gently with the back of the rake and water with a fine rose.
sow.layout: A 20 cm wide band of peas with netting up the middle, then 60 cm before the next band.

care: Mice and birds love peas. Cover with netting or holly until they come up.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Pick pods when they're plump but before the peas go hard.

steps: Put the pea seeds in a cup of lukewarm water and leave them overnight.
Soaking gives faster, more even germination.

plants.name: Runner bean
plants.tip: Keep picking to keep them coming.

sow.title: How to sow
steps: Rake the soil to a fine crumb and pull out any weeds and big stones.
Sow 2 seeds at each spot, 30 cm apart and 5 cm deep.
Put the canes up first, then sow two seeds at the base of each cane.
Cover with soil, firm gently with the back of the rake and water with a fine rose.
When seedlings are big enough to handle, thin them to one every 30 cm.

Water well once flowering starts and mist the flowers in dry spells to help them set.
Thirsty plant. In dry spells give it a deep soak two or three times a week rather than a sprinkle every day.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Pick at about 20 cm before the beans inside start to bulge.
Never let pods ripen on the plant or it stops flowering.

seedSaving.note: Bees can cross runner bean varieties, so grow one variety for pure seed. Only save seed from open-pollinated or heritage varieties. F1 hybrids don't come true from seed.

steps: Leave a few pods at the top to swell and dry on the plant.
Pick before hard frost and finish drying indoors until the pods are papery.
Shell the beans and dry them for another week before storing.

plants.name: French bean
plants.tip: Dwarf types are perfect for small beds and pots.

plants.name: Asparagus

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Dig a trench 30 cm wide and 20 cm deep and make a ridge of soil down the middle.
Sit each crown on top of the ridge and spread the roots out like a spider.
Space them 30 cm apart and cover with 5 cm of soil.
Fill the trench up gradually as the shoots grow through.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: One or two rows down the middle of its own bed.

care: Let all the ferny growth grow in the first two years. Cut it down when it yellows in autumn.
Mulch with compost every spring.
Hungry plant. A liquid feed every two weeks in summer gives a better crop.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Don't cut anything in the first two years.
From year three, cut spears at 15 cm from April until mid June, then let them grow.

plants.name: Globe artichoke
plants.tip: A handsome perennial that crops for years.

steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.

Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.

care: Mulch the crowns with straw in winter in cold spots.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.

care: Earth up the stems and cut them back to 1.5 m in late summer so they don't blow over.

steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Soak the roots of bare-root plants in a bucket for an hour first.
Plant with the crown (where the leaves meet the roots) exactly at soil level. Too deep and it rots, too high and it dries out.
Space them 35 cm apart in rows 75 cm apart.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: Rows or a grid 35 cm apart. Covering the bed with black weed fabric and planting through slits keeps weeds down and fruit clean.

Net against birds once the berries start to colour.
Cut off runners unless you want new plants.

steps: Strawberries are grown from runners rather than seed.

plants.name: Summer raspberry
plants.tip: After fruiting, cut the old canes to the ground and tie in the new ones.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Put a strong post at each end of the row with wires at 60 cm, 1 m and 1.5 m.
Plant canes 45 cm apart with the roots 5 to 8 cm below the surface.
Cut each cane down to 25 cm after planting. It feels harsh but gives strong new canes.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: A single row along a post and wire fence.

care: Mulch every spring with compost.
Tie in new canes to the wires as they grow.
Keep the bed weeded, especially while plants are small.
harvest: Pick when the berries pull off the plug easily.

section.title: How to grow more
steps: Grow new bushes from cuttings rather than seed.
In late autumn cut a pencil-thick stem about 25 cm long from this year's growth.
Push it two thirds deep into a pot of gritty compost or a spare bit of ground and leave it until next autumn.

plants.name: Autumn raspberry
plants.tip: The easiest raspberry. Cut every cane to the ground in February.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Fork over the bed, pull out weeds and work in a bucket of compost per square metre.
Plant canes 45 cm apart with roots 5 to 8 cm deep.
Cut each cane down to 25 cm after planting.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: A row or block. They're shorter so a couple of strings either side is enough support.

care: Cut all canes to the ground every February.
Mulch with compost in spring.

harvest: Pick from late August until the first frosts.

Space bushes 1.5 m apart.

care: Each winter cut out a third of the oldest, darkest stems at the base.

Set the tree so the graft union (the bump low on the stem) is 5 cm above the soil.
Backfill, firm with your boot and tie the tree to the stake.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.

sow.title: How to plant

sow.title: How to sow

Keep the compost damp but never soggy and give them as much light as you can so they don't go leggy.

harden.title: Harden off
steps: About a week before planting out, start getting the plants used to life outside.
Days 1 to 2. Put them out in a sheltered, shady spot for two or three hours and bring them back in.
Days 3 to 5. Leave them out most of the day in brighter light, back in at night.
Days 6 to 7. Leave them out day and night unless frost is forecast.
Going into the tunnel? A few days sitting in the tunnel before planting is enough.
Water them well while they're outside. Pots dry out fast in the wind.

plantOut.title: How to plant out
steps: Water the plants an hour before moving them so the rootball holds together.
Dig a hole a little bigger than the pot and set the plant at the same depth it was growing.
Space them 30 cm apart with rows 30 cm apart.
Firm the soil gently around each plant and water in well.

plants.name: Banana (dwarf, in a pot)
plants.tip: Ireland is too cool for bananas to fruit outside. A dwarf Cavendish in a big pot in a warm conservatory or bright room can fruit after two or three years. The hardy Musa basjoo grows outside in sheltered gardens but its fruit isn't worth eating.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: Buy a young dwarf Cavendish plant. It's far quicker than seed and the fruit will be edible.
Pot it into a large pot with drainage holes, using multipurpose compost mixed with some John Innes No 3 and a handful of grit.
Plant at the same depth it was growing and stand it in the brightest, warmest spot you have, ideally 20 to 30°C and never below 10°C.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: One plant per pot. Give it room, as the leaves spread over a metre.

care: Water generously in summer so the compost never dries out, and mist the leaves on warm days.
Feed every week from spring to autumn with a high nitrogen liquid feed, then switch to tomato feed once a flower stalk appears.
Move it outside to a sheltered sunny spot only in warm summer spells and bring it back in before nights drop below 10°C.
In winter water much less and keep it somewhere bright that stays above 10°C.
Thirsty plant. In dry spells give it a deep soak two or three times a week rather than a sprinkle every day.
harvest: After two or three years a big purple flower stalk appears and small green bananas form behind it. They take three to six months to fill out.
Cut the whole bunch when the fruit is plump and the first one starts to turn yellow, then let them ripen indoors.
The stem that fruited then dies. Cut it down and let one of the young side shoots take its place.

section.title: How to grow more
steps: Bananas you eat have no viable seeds. New plants come from the side shoots (suckers) around the base.
In spring, when a sucker is about 60 cm tall and has its own roots, cut it away from the parent with a sharp spade.
Pot it up on its own and keep it warm until it settles in.

plants.name: Avocado (in a pot)
plants.tip: Ireland is too cool and dull for avocados to crop outside. Grow one as a leafy tree in a pot in a bright room or conservatory. A grafted plant may give a few fruit after three or four years but don't count on it. One grown from a stone makes a lovely houseplant but will rarely fruit.

sow.title: How to plant
steps: For any chance of fruit buy a young grafted plant of a named variety such as Hass. A stone from the shop is fun to grow but takes many years and rarely fruits.
Plant it in a pot with plenty of drainage holes, using multipurpose compost mixed with John Innes No 3 and a couple of handfuls of grit or perlite.
Plant at the same depth it was growing and stand it in the brightest spot you have, out of cold draughts and away from radiators.
Water in well, even if rain is forecast. It settles the soil around the roots.
sow.layout: One plant per pot. It will grow into a small tree, so move it up a pot size every couple of years.

care: Water when the top few centimetres of compost feel dry, then let the excess drain away. Avocados hate soggy roots.
Feed every two weeks from spring to late summer with a balanced liquid feed. Stop feeding in winter.
Pinch out the tip when it reaches about 30 cm, and again later, to make it bushy instead of tall and spindly.
It can go outside to a sheltered sunny spot in warm summer spells. Bring it back in before nights drop below 10°C.
In winter keep it bright, above 10°C and on the dry side. Brown leaf tips usually mean dry air or salty tap water, so use rainwater when you can.
harvest: Flowers appear in spring but fruit only sets now and then indoors. Hand pollinating with a soft brush may help.
Fruit takes six months or more to fill out and does not ripen on the tree.
Pick when full sized and the skin has lost its shine, then leave on a windowsill for a week or two until it gives slightly when pressed.

section.title: How to grow more
steps: Avocados don't come true from the stone and seedlings take ten years or more to fruit, if they ever do. Grow one just for the leaves.
Wash a stone from a ripe avocado and push three cocktail sticks into its sides. Rest it on a glass of water with the pointed end up and the bottom third under water.
Keep it somewhere warm and change the water every few days. Roots and a shoot appear in four to eight weeks, sometimes longer.
When the shoot is about 15 cm tall pot it into compost with the top half of the stone above the surface.
